title: Most Psilocybin Trial Volunteers Can Tell They Got the Real Drug, So Psychiatrists Propose a Multidrug Fake
text:
Most Psilocybin Trial Volunteers Can Tell They Got the Real Drug, So Psychiatrists Propose a Multidrug Fake
A sugar pill cannot mimic a psychedelic trip, and that is becoming a serious problem for psychiatry. In psilocybin studies, volunteers usually know within hours whether they got the real drug, which makes it hard to tell how much of the benefit comes from the drug itself and how much comes from expecting to improve.
On Sept. 16, 2026, psychiatrists from UCSF, UC San Diego, and Stanford proposed an unusual fix in JAMA Psychiatry: build the placebo out of several real, approved drugs so it produces an altered state of its own.
The idea taps into an argument that has simmered in medicine for decades. A fake that feels like nothing may not be a fair comparison for a drug people can feel.
Psychedelic Trials Turned an Old Problem Into an Obvious One
Researchers call the problem unblinding. When participants can guess their treatment, their expectations can shape the results the trial is meant to measure.
Psychedelics make this especially hard to avoid. In an interview with HCPLive, UCSF psychiatrist Josh Woolley, the paper's senior author, said more than 90% of participants in high-dose psilocybin trials correctly identify their treatment, compared with about 60% in antidepressant trials. He added that in most trials, about two-thirds of participants rate the experience among the five most meaningful of their lives.
Researchers have tried active placebos, substances chosen because they cause noticeable sensations. Common choices include niacin, which causes flushing, and the antihistamine diphenhydramine. Neither resembles a psychedelic experience.
The new proposal is called UMBRAA, short for Unidentifiable Multidrug Blinding with Reduced, Authorized Awareness. It would combine carefully chosen FDA-approved drugs from different classes, such as a sedative, a stimulant, and a cannabinoid, to create an unfamiliar altered state. Volunteers would also agree in advance to be told only limited details about what they might receive.
"People say psychedelics can't be masked, so we should stop trying and just move on, because the effects are so obvious," Woolley told UCSF News. "But medicine has been fooled by obvious effects before." He pointed to heart stents for stable chest pain and knee arthroscopy, procedures that looked effective until sham-controlled trials showed otherwise.
The approach has not been tested. "We're also not sure our approach is going to work; it may not be possible," Woolley told HCPLive.
A Burning Nose Spray Showed Why Side Effects Matter
Part of the case rests on a 2024 experiment from Germany that won that year's Ig Nobel Prize in Medicine. MedicalDaily covered it on Wednesday.
Researchers at University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf told volunteers a nasal spray might contain fentanyl. None did. One version contained a trace of capsaicin, the compound that makes chili peppers hot, so it burned. In results published in Brain, about 95% of the 77 participants believed the burning spray contained fentanyl, compared with about 17% for a plain saline spray. Heat pain ratings averaged 26.2 on a 100-point scale after the burning spray and 30.2 after the plain one.
The burn did not dull pain directly. It worked through expectations, especially in people who believed stronger medicines cause more side effects. Turn that around, and a real drug's side effects could make it look better than it is when it is compared with an inert pill.
Two Decades of Mixed Evidence on Active Placebos
The concern predates psychedelic research. A 2004 Cochrane review led by psychiatrist Joanna Moncrieff pooled nine trials with 751 participants that tested older antidepressants against active placebos.
The antidepressants still came out ahead, with a pooled effect of 0.39 standard deviations. But one strongly positive trial drove much of that result. Without it, the effect fell to 0.17, a small difference. The authors wrote that unblinding may inflate antidepressant benefits in trials that use inert placebos.
A broader Cochrane methodology review published in 2023 examined 21 trials with 1,462 participants that included both an active and a standard placebo. In the 14 trials in its main analysis, the difference between the two placebo types was small and not statistically significant.
That did not settle the question. In the five trials judged at low risk of bias, active placebos produced a clearer, statistically significant difference. The authors called the overall result imprecise and urged trialists to think carefully about placebo choice when unblinding is likely. Active placebos did not drive more people to drop out, and the review found no clear link between how well an active placebo mimicked a drug and how much it changed results.
The Limits of Faking Side Effects
Active placebos have their own costs. In the 2023 Cochrane review, participants given active placebos had about three times the odds of reporting adverse events as those given standard placebos. Mixing several drugs to imitate a psychedelic raises further safety and ethics questions, which the UMBRAA authors say would require careful drug selection, screening, and safeguards.
The Hamburg experiment has limits too. It involved healthy young adults, brief laboratory heat, a modest effect, and deliberate deception, and it did not test any real medication.
None of this means real medicines do not work, or that a drug with stronger side effects is a better drug. It means the way a trial is built can shape how large a benefit appears. Patients with questions about a medication's effects should talk with their prescriber rather than stopping or changing treatment on their own.
Key Questions Answered
What is an active placebo?
It is a fake treatment that produces noticeable sensations, unlike a sugar pill, so participants find it harder to tell whether they received the real drug.
Why are psychedelic trials hard to blind?
Psilocybin's effects are unmistakable. Josh Woolley of UCSF estimates that more than 90% of participants in high-dose psilocybin trials correctly identify their treatment.
What is the UMBRAA proposal?
Published in JAMA Psychiatry on Sept. 16, 2026, it would combine several FDA-approved drugs from different classes into one placebo and limit what volunteers are told. It has not been tested.
What did the burning nasal spray experiment show?
Volunteers who felt a capsaicin burn reported slightly less heat pain than after a plain spray, mostly because the burn convinced them they had received fentanyl.
Do active placebos change trial results?
Possibly. A 2023 Cochrane review of 21 trials found no significant overall difference, but trials at low risk of bias showed a clearer gap. The evidence is uncertain.
Should patients worry their medicines do not work?
No. The research concerns how benefits are measured. Anyone with medication questions should talk with their prescriber.
